title: Preprocedure Verification and Time-Out: Stop Before the Wrong Procedure Starts
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Wrong-person, wrong-site and wrong-procedure events are prevented by layered verification, not memory. The PN/LVN should stop the process and escalate any mismatch in identity, consent, procedure, site, laterality, implants, allergies or required preparation before the procedure proceeds.
recognize: A discrepancy between the schedule, consent, patient statement, site mark, imaging or team plan is a safety stop.
The final time-out occurs immediately before the procedure with active team participation; it is not a checkbox completed earlier in the day.
priorities: Use approved identifiers and verify required documents/site/equipment according to policy.
Speak up and stop progression when information conflicts or is missing.
assessMonitor: Confirm patient identity, procedure/site, consent status, allergies, relevant imaging, implants/equipment and preparation within assigned role.
interventions: Participate in preprocedure verification and time-out as required, maintaining a sterile/safe pause until discrepancies are resolved.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants, insulin, sedatives, antibiotics and allergy information must be reconciled with the procedural plan rather than assumed from a generic pre-op list.
redFlags: Missing critical equipment or allergy information
teaching: Patients should expect repeated identity/procedure questions; repetition is a safety feature, not a sign that the team is confused.
delegationScope: The exact PN/LVN role in verification and time-out varies by facility; no staff member should ignore an unresolved safety discrepancy.
examTrap: Proceeding because 'everyone knows which side' when the documentation and site mark disagree.
oneLinePearl: When identifiers disagree, the procedure stops—not the questioning.
sourceBasis: Joint Commission Universal Protocol and 2026 National Performance Goals

title: Postoperative Airway and Breathing: Sedation Can Hide Deterioration
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: In the early postoperative period, airway obstruction, residual anesthetic effects, opioids, aspiration, atelectasis and bleeding can rapidly compromise breathing. New snoring obstruction, hypoventilation, rising oxygen need, somnolence or stridor requires immediate reassessment and escalation.
recognize: A patient may maintain SpO2 temporarily on supplemental oxygen while ventilation worsens.
Stridor, paradoxical breathing, weak cough, pooling secretions or inability to stay awake are high-risk findings.
priorities: Assess airway patency, respiratory effort, sedation level and oxygen device; position and support airway/breathing within orders while escalating deterioration.
Do not attribute profound somnolence to 'normal anesthesia recovery' without evaluating ventilation.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory rate/depth, effort, SpO2, sedation, airway sounds, pain medication timing and response.
interventions: Use prescribed oxygen, positioning, airway maneuvers/equipment and reversal/emergency pathways according to competency and protocol.
medicationSafety: Opioids, benzodiazepines and residual anesthetics can have additive respiratory-depressant effects.
teaching: Patients should request help before ambulating while sedated and report severe breathlessness or throat swelling/noisy breathing.
delegationScope: Routine postoperative observations may be shared; evaluation of airway/breathing deterioration requires licensed-nurse action and escalation.
examTrap: Increasing oxygen without addressing worsening hypoventilation and sedation.
oneLinePearl: Oxygen can mask hypoventilation; watch breathing and consciousness too.
sourceBasis: Joint Commission 2026 National Performance Goals on monitoring changes in condition and resuscitation readiness

title: Postoperative Hemorrhage: Trend Perfusion Before the Hemoglobin Catches Up
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Postoperative bleeding may be external, drain-visible or concealed. Tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, cool skin, oliguria, increasing pain/swelling, mental-status change or rapidly increasing drain output can precede a dramatic hemoglobin drop.
recognize: A stable initial hemoglobin does not exclude acute blood loss.
Hidden bleeding may appear as abdominal distention, flank/back pain, wound swelling or unexplained shock.
priorities: Assess ABCs/perfusion, wound/dressings/drains and vital-sign trends; escalate suspected hemorrhage immediately.
Maintain ordered IV access/support and prepare for urgent diagnostics/transfusion/procedure according to team plan.
assessMonitor: Trend HR/BP, mental status, skin/perfusion, urine output, wound/drain output, abdominal girth or site swelling and ordered labs.
interventions: Apply ordered pressure/support, maintain NPO when reintervention is possible, and follow hemorrhage escalation protocols.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulants, antiplatelets and recent heparin/NSAID exposure; do not independently give reversal agents without protocol/order.
teaching: Report sudden swelling, heavy drainage, faintness, racing heart or increasing weakness promptly.
delegationScope: Drain measurement may be delegated with thresholds; interpretation and emergency escalation remain licensed responsibilities.
examTrap: Waiting for a low hemoglobin before treating clinical shock as postoperative bleeding.
oneLinePearl: Acute hemorrhage is a perfusion problem before it becomes a lab-number problem.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. postoperative hemorrhage and patient-safety principles

title: Surgical-Site Infection Prevention: Clean Technique Is a Whole-Pathway Job
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: SSI prevention spans preoperative preparation, antimicrobial timing by the procedural team, aseptic technique, glucose/temperature management when relevant, clean wound care and early recognition of infection. Postoperative redness alone is not enough—trend the wound and systemic pattern.
recognize: Increasing pain, spreading erythema, purulent drainage, wound separation, fever or systemic deterioration can indicate infection.
Some high-risk patients may show subtle findings, so worsening function or delirium can matter.
priorities: Perform hand hygiene and ordered wound care using required aseptic technique.
Escalate purulent drainage, spreading infection, wound separation or systemic illness promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend incision appearance, drainage, pain, temperature, glucose when ordered and systemic signs.
interventions: Protect the incision, maintain dressing/hand-hygiene standards and reinforce wound-care/discharge instructions.
medicationSafety: Prophylactic antibiotics are procedure-timed therapies; do not continue or restart them independently because a wound looks red.
teaching: Keep the incision clean/dry as instructed and report increasing redness, drainage, fever, separation or worsening pain.
delegationScope: Wound care may be performed within competency/policy; assessment of suspected infection and plan changes require licensed/team escalation.
examTrap: Starting leftover antibiotics at home instead of reporting a worsening surgical wound.
oneLinePearl: SSI prevention starts before incision and continues after discharge.
sourceBasis: CDC Guideline for Prevention of Surgical Site Infection and 2026 NHSN SSI resources

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention and Catheters: Scan Before You Recatheterize
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Postoperative urinary retention can follow anesthesia, opioids, immobility and bladder dysfunction. Assess voiding, suprapubic fullness, discomfort and bladder volume per protocol; avoid prolonged indwelling catheter use when no indication remains because infection risk rises with catheter exposure.
recognize: Small frequent voids do not exclude retention.
Agitation or delirium in an older postoperative patient can be worsened by a distended bladder.
priorities: Assess time since voiding, intake, symptoms and bladder volume per protocol before reflex catheterization.
Remove postoperative catheters promptly when the indication has ended according to orders/protocol and escalate persistent retention.
assessMonitor: Trend voided volume, bladder scan/residual if ordered, discomfort, urine characteristics, catheter indication and signs of infection.
interventions: Support mobility/privacy/positioning and ordered bladder protocol; maintain a closed drainage system when a catheter is required.
medicationSafety: Opioids and anticholinergic medications can worsen retention; review exposure when voiding changes.
teaching: Report inability to void, severe lower-abdominal pressure, fever or new urinary symptoms after surgery.
delegationScope: Routine urine measurement may be delegated; bladder-scan use/catheterization depend on policy/competency and interpretation requires licensed oversight.
examTrap: Leaving a postoperative catheter in place 'for convenience' after its indication has ended.
oneLinePearl: A catheter solves retention only if it is still needed—and every extra day adds risk.

title: Postoperative VTE Prevention: Mobility, Prophylaxis, and New Symptoms
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Health Promotion and Maintenance
bottomLine: Surgery and hospitalization increase VTE risk. Prevention is individualized and may include early mobility, mechanical devices and prescribed anticoagulant prophylaxis; sudden dyspnea, chest pain, syncope or new unilateral limb swelling requires immediate escalation.
recognize: VTE risk changes with immobility, prior VTE, cancer, age, surgery type and bleeding risk.
DVT can present with unilateral swelling/pain, while PE may present with sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, syncope or hypoxemia.
priorities: Apply ordered mechanical/pharmacologic prophylaxis correctly and mobilize as prescribed.
Escalate possible PE immediately and do not massage a painful swollen limb.
assessMonitor: Trend mobility, limb symptoms, respiratory symptoms, bleeding risk and adherence to prophylaxis.
interventions: Assist early ambulation, ensure compression devices are functioning when ordered and administer prophylaxis safely.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant prophylaxis requires bleeding surveillance and procedure timing awareness; do not hold or double doses without direction.
redFlags: New unilateral swelling with cardiopulmonary symptoms
teaching: Move as directed, use compression devices correctly and report sudden breathing/chest symptoms or one-sided swelling promptly.
delegationScope: Ambulation assistance and device checks may be delegated; interpretation of VTE/bleeding symptoms requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Massaging a postoperative calf that is newly swollen and painful.
oneLinePearl: Prevent the clot early; treat sudden chest/breathing symptoms as an emergency.

title: Postoperative Pulmonary Expansion: Move, Breathe, Reassess
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Postoperative pulmonary prevention is multimodal: adequate analgesia, repositioning, early mobility, coughing/deep breathing and prescribed lung-expansion strategies. An incentive spirometer is a tool—not a substitute for assessing worsening respiratory status.
recognize: Shallow breathing, pain-limited cough, immobility and sedation increase atelectasis and secretion-retention risk.
Fever, increasing oxygen need, dyspnea or focal deterioration requires evaluation beyond simply increasing spirometer use.
priorities: Control pain enough to allow movement/breathing, mobilize as ordered and reinforce correct technique for prescribed exercises/devices.
Escalate increasing oxygen requirement, respiratory distress or altered mentation.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory effort, breath sounds, SpO2, cough/secretions, mobility, pain and sedation.
interventions: Reposition, assist ambulation, coach coughing/deep breathing and use incentive spirometry when prescribed as part of the broader plan.
medicationSafety: Balance analgesia with respiratory/sedation monitoring; uncontrolled pain and oversedation can both impair pulmonary recovery.
redFlags: Marked asymmetry or absent breath sounds
teaching: Use the breathing device exactly as taught, but also get out of bed/move and report worsening breathlessness.
delegationScope: Mobility and breathing coaching may be delegated within the plan; evaluation of respiratory deterioration remains licensed.
examTrap: Treating every postoperative low-grade fever with more incentive spirometry without assessing the patient.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary recovery needs movement, pain control, deep breathing—and clinical reassessment.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. postoperative pulmonary-complication prevention principles

title: Surgical Drains: Follow Output, Patency, and the Wound
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Drain care requires secure placement, ordered suction/compression, accurate output trends and wound assessment. Sudden high bloody output, abrupt cessation with swelling/pain, loss of suction, accidental removal or foul drainage can signal a complication.
recognize: Expected drainage usually trends down and changes character over time according to procedure.
No output is not automatically reassuring if the site is swelling or the patient is worsening.
priorities: Keep tubing unkinked/secured and the collection system functioning as designed.
Escalate sudden large bloody output, blocked-drain signs, accidental dislodgement or infection.
assessMonitor: Trend amount/color/character, insertion site, suction/compression, tubing patency, pain, swelling and systemic signs.
interventions: Empty/measure and recharge closed-suction devices according to policy, maintain clean/aseptic technique and secure tubing.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants can alter the significance of new bloody drainage and should be included in the assessment.
redFlags: Sudden no output with expanding swelling
teaching: At home, record output as instructed and report sudden changes, fever, severe pain or drain dislodgement.
delegationScope: Drain emptying/measurement may be performed within competency; interpreting abnormal trends and changing/removing drains require appropriate licensed/provider authority.
examTrap: Documenting zero drain output as improvement while the surgical site is rapidly enlarging.
oneLinePearl: A drain trend matters only when you also look at the patient and the wound.

title: Wound Dehiscence and Evisceration: Protect, Position, Escalate
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Dehiscence is separation of surgical wound layers; evisceration is protrusion of internal organs and is an emergency. Protect exposed tissue with sterile saline-moistened dressings per protocol, reduce strain, keep the patient NPO and obtain immediate surgical help—never push organs back inside.
recognize: A sudden 'popping' sensation, increased serosanguineous drainage or visible wound separation may precede evisceration.
Coughing, vomiting, infection, poor healing and increased intra-abdominal pressure can contribute.
priorities: Stay with the patient, call for urgent help, position to reduce abdominal strain and cover exposed tissue with sterile saline-moistened material according to protocol.
Keep NPO and prepare for urgent operative management.
assessMonitor: Monitor wound, vital signs, pain, exposed tissue perfusion and signs of shock/infection.
interventions: Do not attempt to reinsert organs; maintain sterile protection and minimize tension/coughing/straining while help arrives.
medicationSafety: Give analgesia/antiemetic therapy only as ordered while maintaining emergency priorities and NPO status.
redFlags: Severe abdominal pain with wound change
teaching: Support the incision when coughing and report sudden drainage, opening or a popping sensation immediately.
delegationScope: This emergency requires licensed-nurse assessment/escalation; assistive staff can summon help and bring supplies.
examTrap: Trying to gently replace protruding bowel into the abdomen.

title: Postoperative Hypothermia: Warm Safely and Watch the Consequences
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Perioperative hypothermia can worsen shivering, oxygen demand, coagulation and recovery. Rewarm with approved active/passive methods, monitor temperature and hemodynamics, and investigate persistent or severe hypothermia rather than treating it as a comfort issue only.
recognize: Shivering increases metabolic/oxygen demand; older, small, pediatric and prolonged-procedure patients may cool rapidly.
Persistent hypothermia can coexist with bleeding, sepsis, endocrine disease or exposure and deserves broader assessment.
priorities: Verify core/appropriate temperature measurement, apply ordered warming and reassess circulation/respiratory status.
Escalate severe hypothermia, arrhythmia, ongoing bleeding or failure to rewarm.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, shivering, HR/BP/rhythm, oxygenation, skin condition under warming devices and bleeding.
interventions: Use approved forced-air/blanket/fluid-warming strategies according to setting and protect skin from thermal injury.
medicationSafety: Sedation/anesthesia impair thermoregulation; medication effects and delayed metabolism may persist during hypothermia.
teaching: Report severe chills, numbness, dizziness or feeling unusually cold after discharge when accompanied by other symptoms.
delegationScope: Temperature collection and approved warming assistance may be delegated; interpretation of severe/persistent hypothermia requires licensed assessment.
examTrap: Applying an unregulated direct heat source to speed warming and causing burns.
oneLinePearl: Warm the patient, protect the skin, and ask why they are still cold.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. perioperative temperature-management and patient-safety principles
